abstract: The practical application of high-entropy alloy (HEA) electrocatalysts that support the acidic hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) is often limited by poor active-site accessibility and a need for binders, conductive additives, and external supports. Herein, an etched porous MnFeCoNiCu HEA electrode was developed as a self-supported acidic HER electrocatalyst. The process features mechanical alloying, poly(methyl methacrylate) (PMMA)-assisted pore formation, and electrochemical etching. The porous framework enhances both electrolyte accessibility and active-site utilization, and electrochemical etching generates a roughened surface with an enlarged electrochemically accessible interface. Systematic control of the pore architecture reveals that HER activity is governed not simply by porosity but, rather, by the balance between pore connectivity and framework continuity. Among the various investigated structures, an electrode prepared using an HEA-to-PMMA ratio of 2:1 exhibited the most favorable architecture and delivered overpotentials of 76.7 and 173.8 mV at − 10 and − 50 mA cm − 2 , respectively, with a Tafel slope of 76.1 mV dec − 1 . Operation was stable over 100 h in 0.5 M H 2 SO 4 . Post-stability analyses confirm that the porous HEA framework remains intact after prolonged acidic HER operation. This work demonstrates that the synergistic combination of pore-architecture engineering and electrochemical surface activation is an effective strategy when developing self-supported HEA electrocatalysts for acidic hydrogen production.

abstract: Oxygen electrocatalysis, mainly including the oxygen reduction reaction (ORR) and oxygen evolution reaction (OER), is a cornerstone in rechargeable metal–air batteries. However, these reactions are sluggish due to the four-electron transfer process and the linear scaling relationship of the intermediate binding strength. Herein, we have rationally developed a hybrid composite consisting of high-entropy alloy nanoparticles (NPs) encapsulated in carbon nanotubes (CNTs) to significantly improve the electrocatalytic performance. In situ spectroscopy investigations and theoretical calculations disclose that high-entropy alloys undergo dynamic reconstruction to form MOOH and M–OH (M represents metallic elements) as the authentic active species in the ORR and OER processes, respectively. Specifically, Fe, Co, Mn, and Cu regulate the charge transfer between the Ni–O bonds in MOOH for the OER, while the high-entropy effect and surface-absorbed OH groups coregulate the d-band center of surface Co for the efficient ORR. Accordingly, the as-developed FeCoNiMnCu@CNTs exhibits activity for both ORR and OER, with an ultralow voltage gap of 0.626 V between the half-wave potential of ORR and the OER potential at 10 mA cm –2 . Moreover, Zn–air batteries with FeCoNiMnCu@CNTs exhibit a power density of 131.3 mW cm –2 and robust stability.

abstract: High-entropy alloy (HEA) nanocatalysts offer exceptional compositional flexibility for electrocatalysis, yet their nanoscale synthesis is constrained by a thermodynamic–kinetic conflict: high temperatures required for entropic stabilization promote sintering, while asynchronous reduction of multicomponent precursors induces premature phase segregation. Here, we demonstrate a ligand-mediated strategy that addresses this conflict by employing 1,10-phenanthroline to coordinate disparate metal precursors. This interaction significantly retards the reduction onset, shifting nucleation into a narrow, high-temperature window where rapid atomic diffusion enables fast alloying. Simultaneously, the ligand’s in situ carbonization generates an atomically thin, chemically bonded N-doped carbon layer that kinetically confines nanoparticle growth and stabilizes the single-phase solid-solution phase against surface-energy-driven sintering. Distinct from physical barriers that passively isolate, the chemically coupled HEA–carbon interface functions as an active armor that enhances catalytic functionality by electronically modulating the HEA core and reshaping the local reaction microenvironment through regulated interfacial solvent organization and reactant accessibility. As a result, phase-pure ∼2.7 nm PtRuCuCoNi nanoparticles exhibit high oxygen reduction activity and durability, delivering a peak power density of 1.92 W cm –2 and maintaining stable operation for 100 h at a high current density of 1 A cm –2 in an anion-exchange membrane fuel cell. This work illustrates how integrating reduction retardation with chemically active encapsulation can transform stability constraints into functional advantages, offering a general strategy for resilient multicomponent nanomaterials.
